blocks.p: When they had talked a little longer, they came near a house that stood beside the road, a house built for the relief of pilgrims, as is told more fully in the First Part of these records. It was the house of the Interpreter. As they came up to the door they heard a great deal of talk inside, and when they listened, they thought they heard Christiana mentioned by name. For you must know that word of her and her children going on pilgrimage had run ahead of her; and it pleased the people of the house all the more because they had heard that she was Christian’s wife, the woman who had once been so unwilling to hear of pilgrimage at all. So the travelers stood still and listened to the good people inside praising her, never dreaming she stood at the door. At last Christiana knocked, as she had knocked at the gate before. A young girl named Innocent came and opened the door, and there were two women standing on the step.
“Who is it you want to speak with here?” said the girl.

“We understand,” Christiana answered, “that this is a place set apart for those who have become pilgrims, and we at your door are pilgrims now. So we ask to share in what we have come for; the day, as you see, is nearly over, and we would rather not go any further tonight.”
“May I have your name, so that I can tell my Lord inside?”
“My name is Christiana. I was the wife of the pilgrim who traveled this way some years ago, and these are his four children. This young woman is my companion, and she is going on pilgrimage too.”

Then Innocent ran inside and said to the others, “Can you guess who is at the door? Christiana and her children, and her companion, all waiting to be taken in!” They leaped for joy and went and told their Master. He came to the door, looked at her, and said, “Are you the Christiana whom Christian, that good man, left behind when he took up a pilgrim’s life?”

“I am the woman who was so hard-hearted that I made light of my husband’s troubles and left him to go on his journey alone, and these are his four children. But now I have come too, for I am convinced that no way is right but this one.”

“Then what was written of the man who said to his son, ‘Go, work today in my vineyard,’ is fulfilled in you,” said the Interpreter. “’He answered, I will not; but afterward he repented and went.’” [Matt. 21:29]
“So be it. Amen,” said Christiana. “God make it a true saying of me, and grant that at the last I may be found by him in peace, without spot, and blameless.”

“But why are you standing out there at the door? Come in, daughter of Abraham. We were talking of you just now, for news reached us before you did that you had become a pilgrim. Come, children, come in; come, young woman, come in.” So he brought them all into the house.

Once inside, they were told to sit down and rest; and when they had, the people who served the pilgrims in that house came into the room to see them. One smiled, and another smiled, and all of them smiled for joy that Christiana had become a pilgrim. They looked at the boys too, and stroked their faces with their hands as a sign of welcome. They were just as loving to Mercy, and bade them all welcome to their Master’s house.

After a while, since supper was not yet ready, the Interpreter took them into his rooms of emblems and showed them what Christian, Christiana’s husband, had seen there some time before: the man in the cage, the man and his dream, the man who cut his way through his enemies, and the portrait of the greatest of them all, with the rest of the things that had done Christian so much good.

When Christiana and her company had taken all this in, the Interpreter led them aside again, first into a room where there was a man who could look no way but downward, with a muck-rake in his hand. Above his head stood One holding a heavenly crown, offering him the crown in exchange for the rake; but the man never looked up or paid any attention. He went on raking up the straws, the small sticks, and the dust of the floor.
“I think I understand something of this,” said Christiana. “This is a picture of a man of this world, isn’t it, sir?”

“You have said it exactly,” said the Interpreter. “His muck-rake shows his earthbound mind. And when you see him paying more attention to raking up straws and sticks and the dust of the floor than to the One who calls to him from above with the heavenly crown in his hand, it is to show that to some people heaven is only a fable, and the things of this world are the only things that count as real. And as you saw, the man could look no way but downward: that is to teach you that when earthly things get power over men’s minds, they carry their hearts clean away from God.”
“Oh, deliver me from this muck-rake!” said Christiana.

“That prayer,” said the Interpreter, “has lain by until it is almost rusty. ‘Give me not riches’ is scarcely the prayer of one man in ten thousand. [Prov. 30:8] Straws and sticks and dust are the great things most people go after now.” At that Mercy and Christiana wept, and said, “It is true. It is sadly true.”

When the Interpreter had shown them this, he brought them into the very best room in the house, and a splendid room it was. He told them to look around and see whether they could find anything there worth learning. They looked round and round, but there was nothing to be seen except a very large spider on the wall, and that they passed over.
“Sir, I see nothing,” said Mercy; but Christiana held her peace.
“Look again,” said the Interpreter.
So Mercy looked again and said, “There is nothing here but an ugly spider, hanging by her hands on the wall.”
“Is there only one spider in all this spacious room?” he said.

Then the tears stood in Christiana’s eyes, for she was a woman quick to understand, and she said, “Yes, Lord, there is more than one here; and spiders whose venom is far more deadly than hers.” The Interpreter looked at her kindly and said, “You have spoken the truth.” At that Mercy blushed and the boys covered their faces, for now they all began to understand the riddle.

“’The spider takes hold with her hands,’ as you see, ‘and is in kings’ palaces,’” said the Interpreter. [Prov. 30:28] “And why is that written down, except to show you that however full of the venom of sin you may be, you may still, by the hand of faith, take hold and live in the best room of the King’s house above?”

“I thought of something like this,” said Christiana, “but I couldn’t work it all out. I thought that we were like spiders, ugly creatures however fine the room we are in; but that this spider, this venomous and ill-favored creature, should teach us how to act in faith never entered my mind. And yet she has taken hold with her hands, as I see, and she lives in the best room in the house. God has made nothing in vain.”
Then they all seemed glad, though the tears stood in their eyes; and they looked at one another, and bowed before the Interpreter.

Next he brought them into a room where there was a hen with her chicks, and told them to watch a while. One of the chicks went to the trough to drink, and every time she drank she lifted her head and her eyes toward heaven. “See what this little chick does,” he said, “and learn from her to acknowledge where your mercies come from, by receiving them with your eyes lifted up. Now look again,” he said; and they watched, and saw that the hen dealt with her chicks in four different ways. First, she had a common call, which she used all day long. Second, she had a special call, which she used only sometimes. Third, she had a brooding note. And fourth, she had a cry of alarm. [Matt. 23:37]

“Now compare this hen to your King,” he said, “and these chicks to his obedient ones. For like her, he has his ways of dealing with his people. By his common call he gives nothing; by his special call he always has something to give; he has a brooding voice for those who are under his wing; and he has a cry of alarm to warn them when he sees the enemy coming. I chose to lead you into the room where such things are, my dear ones, because you are women, and these are easy for you.”
“Sir,” said Christiana, “please let us see some more.”

So he brought them into the slaughterhouse, where a butcher was killing a sheep; and the sheep was quiet, and took her death patiently. “You must learn from this sheep,” said the Interpreter, “to suffer, and to put up with wrongs without grumbling or complaint. See how quietly she takes her death, and without protest lets her skin be pulled over her ears. Your King calls you his sheep.”

After this he led them into his garden, where there was a great variety of flowers. “Do you see all these?” he said. Christiana said yes. “See how the flowers differ in height, in quality, in color, in scent, and in virtue, and some are better than others; and yet where the gardener has set them, there they stand, and do not quarrel with one another.”

Then he brought them into his field, which he had sown with wheat and corn; but when they looked, the heads of all the plants had been cut off, and only the straw remained. “This ground was manured, and plowed, and sown,” he said. “But what shall we do with the crop?”
“Burn some,” said Christiana, “and make muck of the rest.”

“Fruit, you see, is the thing you look for,” said the Interpreter, “and for want of it you condemn the crop to the fire, and to be trodden under men’s feet. Take care that in this you do not condemn yourselves.”

As they were coming back in from outside, they noticed a little robin with a great spider in his beak. “Look here,” said the Interpreter. They looked, and Mercy wondered at it; but Christiana said, “What a disgrace for such a pretty little bird as the robin redbreast, a bird above most others, who loves to keep a kind of friendship with man. I had thought they lived on crumbs of bread, or on some such harmless food. I like him less than I did.”

“This robin,” the Interpreter replied, “is a very apt emblem of some who profess faith. To look at, they are like this robin: pretty in their note, their color, and their bearing. They seem to have a great love for sincere believers, and above all others to want their company and to keep it, as if they could live on the good man’s crumbs. They claim that this is why they frequent the houses of the godly and the appointed meetings of the Lord; but when they are by themselves, like the robin, they can catch and gobble up spiders. They can change their diet, drink iniquity, and swallow down sin like water.”
When they had come back into the house, and supper was still not ready, Christiana asked the Interpreter to show or tell them some other things that would do them good. So he began.
“The fatter the sow, the more she wants the mire; the fatter the ox, the more playfully he goes to the slaughter; and the healthier the strong man, the more prone he is to evil.
“Women have a desire to go neat and fine, and it is a lovely thing to be adorned with what is of great price in God’s sight.
“It is easier to keep watch for a night or two than to sit up a whole year together; so it is easier to begin to profess faith well than to hold out as one should to the end.
“Every ship’s master in a storm will gladly throw overboard whatever is of least value in the vessel; but who throws the best out first? Only the man who does not fear God.
“One leak will sink a ship, and one sin will destroy a sinner.
“He who forgets his friend is ungrateful to him; but he who forgets his Savior is unmerciful to himself.
“He who lives in sin and looks for happiness hereafter is like a man who sows weeds and expects to fill his barn with wheat or barley.
“If a man wants to live well, let him bring his last day to him, and keep it always for company.
“Whispering and shifting thoughts prove that sin is in the world.
“If the world, which God sets little store by, counts for so much with men, what must heaven be, which God commends?
“If this life, hedged about with so many troubles, is so hard for us to let go of, what is the life above?
“Everyone will cry up the goodness of men; but who is there who is moved, as he should be, by the goodness of God?
“We seldom sit down to a meal without eating and leaving some; so there is in Jesus Christ more merit and righteousness than the whole world has need of.”

When the Interpreter had finished, he took them out into his garden again and brought them to a tree whose inside was all rotten and gone, though it still grew and bore leaves. “What does this mean?” said Mercy. “This tree,” he said, “whose outside is fair and whose inside is rotten, is like many who are in the garden of God. With their mouths they speak high things on God’s behalf, but in fact they will do nothing for him. Their leaves are fair, but their hearts are good for nothing but tinder for the devil’s tinderbox.”

Now supper was ready, the table spread, and everything set out; so when one of them had given thanks, they sat down and ate. The Interpreter usually entertained those who lodged with him with music at meals, so the minstrels played; and there was one who sang, and a very fine voice he had. This was his song:

v: The Lord alone is my support,
by him alone I’m fed;
how then can I lack anything,
or go without my bread?

blocks.p: When the song and the music were over, the Interpreter asked Christiana what it was that first moved her to take up a pilgrim’s life.

“First,” Christiana answered, “the loss of my husband came to my mind, and I grieved for him with all my heart; but that was only natural affection. Then after that, my husband’s troubles and his pilgrimage came to mind, and how like a boor I had behaved toward him over it. So guilt took hold of me, and would have dragged me down into the pond, if I had not just then had a dream of my husband’s well-being, and a letter sent me by the King of the country where he lives, calling me to come to him. The dream and the letter together worked so on my mind that they drove me onto this road.”
“But did you meet with no opposition before you got out of your door?”

“Yes. A neighbor of mine, one Mrs. Timid (she was kin to the man who would have persuaded my husband to turn back, for fear of the lions), made a complete fool of me, as she put it, for my desperate adventure. She did all she could to discourage me from it, with the hardships and troubles my husband had met on the way; but all that I got over well enough. What has troubled me far more is a dream I had of two ugly-looking men, who I thought were plotting how to make me fail in my journey. It still runs in my mind, and makes me afraid of everyone I meet, in case they mean to do me harm and turn me out of the way. Indeed, I may tell my Lord, though I would not want everyone to know it, that between this house and the gate where we came into the way, we were both so badly assaulted that we were made to cry out, Murder! And the two who attacked us were like the two I saw in my dream.”
“Your beginning is good,” said the Interpreter; “your latter end shall greatly increase.” Then he turned to Mercy and said, “And what moved you to come here, dear heart?”
Mercy blushed and trembled, and for a while said nothing.
“Don’t be afraid,” he said. “Only believe, and speak your mind.”

“Truly, sir,” she began, “it is my lack of experience that makes me want to keep silent, and that also fills me with fears of coming short at the last. I cannot tell of visions and dreams as my friend Christiana can, and I do not know what it is to grieve over refusing the counsel of good relations.”
“What was it, then, dear heart, that persuaded you to do what you have done?”

“Why, when our friend here was packing up to leave our town, another woman and I happened to go and see her. We knocked at the door and went in, and when we saw what she was doing, we asked what she meant by it. She said she had been sent for, to go to her husband; and then she stood up and told us how she had seen him in a dream, living in a wonderful place among immortals, wearing a crown, playing on a harp, eating and drinking at his Prince’s table, and singing praises to him for bringing him there. Now while she was telling us these things, my heart burned within me, and I said in my heart, If this is true, I will leave my father and my mother and the land of my birth, and if I may, I will go with Christiana. So I asked her more about the truth of these things, and whether she would let me go with her; for I saw now that there was no living in our town any longer except in danger of ruin. Yet I came away with a heavy heart; not because I was unwilling to come, but because so many of my relations were left behind. And I have come with all the desire of my heart, and I will go, if I may, with Christiana, to her husband and his King.”

“Your setting out is good,” said the Interpreter, “for you have believed the truth. You are a Ruth, who for the love she bore to Naomi and to the Lord her God left father and mother and the land of her birth, to go out with a people she had not known before. ‘The Lord repay your work, and a full reward be given you by the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to trust.’” [Ruth 2:12]

Now supper was over, and beds were prepared; the women were laid in rooms of their own, and the boys by themselves. When Mercy was in bed she could not sleep for joy, because her fears of missing the end at last were now further from her than they had ever been. So she lay there blessing and praising God, who had shown her such favor.

In the morning they rose with the sun and got ready to leave; but the Interpreter would have them wait a while. “You must leave this house in proper order,” he said. Then he said to the girl who had first opened the door to them, “Take them into the garden to the bath, and wash them there, and make them clean from the soil they have picked up in traveling.” So Innocent took them into the garden and brought them to the bath, and told them that there they must wash and be clean, for her Master would have every woman who called at his house on pilgrimage do so. They went in and washed, the women and the boys and all; and they came out of that bath not only sweet and clean, but much refreshed and strengthened in every joint. When they came back in, they looked a good deal fairer than when they had gone out to wash.

When they had returned from the bath in the garden, the Interpreter looked at them and said, “Fair as the moon.” Then he called for the seal with which those who had washed in his bath were always sealed. The seal was brought, and he set his mark on them, so that they would be known in the places they had still to go. The seal was the substance and sum of the Passover that the children of Israel ate when they came out of the land of Egypt, and the mark was set between their eyes. [Exod. 13:8-10] It added greatly to their beauty, for it was an ornament to their faces; it added to their gravity too, and made their faces more like the faces of angels.

Then the Interpreter said to the girl who was waiting on the women, “Go into the vestry and fetch out garments for these people.” She went and fetched white robes and laid them down before him, and he told them to put them on. “It was fine linen, white and clean.” When the women were dressed in them, each one seemed almost to stand in awe of the other; for neither could see the glory on herself that she could see on her companion, and so they began to think better of each other than of themselves. “You are fairer than I am,” said one; “and you are more lovely than I am,” said the other. The children too stood amazed at the state they had been brought to.

Then the Interpreter called for one of his servants, a man named Great-heart, and told him to take sword and helmet and shield. “Take these daughters of mine,” he said, “and conduct them to the house called Beautiful, where they will rest next.” So Great-heart took up his weapons and went ahead of them, and the Interpreter said, “God speed.” The rest of the household sent them off with many a good wish. So they went on their way, singing:

v: This house has been our second stage;
here we have heard and seen
those good things which, from age to age,
hid from the world have been.
The muck-raker, the spider, hen,
and chicken, taught to me
a lesson each; and let me then
shaped by that lesson be.
The butcher, garden, and the field,
the robin and his bait,
the rotten tree as well, all yield
me arguments of weight;
to move me on to watch and pray,
to strive to be sincere,
to take my cross up day by day,
and serve the Lord with fear.

blocks.p: Now I saw in my dream that they went on, with Great-heart ahead of them, until they came to the place where Christian’s burden fell off his back and tumbled into a tomb. Here they paused, and here too they blessed God.

“Now it comes to my mind,” said Christiana, “what was said to us at the gate: that we should have pardon by word and by deed. By word, that is, by the promise; by deed, that is, in the way it was obtained. Of the promise I know something; but what it is to have pardon by deed, or in the way it was obtained, I suppose you know, Mr. Great-heart. If you would, let us hear you speak about it.”

“Pardon by deed,” said Great-heart, “is pardon won by someone for another who needs it; not by the person who is pardoned, but, as the One who gives it might say, in the way in which I obtained it. So, to answer your question more fully: the pardon that you and Mercy and these boys have received was obtained by another, by the One who let you in at the gate; and he obtained it in two ways at once. He lived out a perfect righteousness to cover you, and he shed his blood to wash you in.”
“But if he gives his righteousness to us, what will he have left for himself?”
“He has more righteousness than you have need of, or than he needs himself.”
“Please, show me how.”

“With all my heart. But first I must say this: the One we are about to speak of has no equal. He has two natures in one Person, plain to tell apart, impossible to divide. To each of these natures belongs a righteousness, and each righteousness is essential to its nature, so that you could as easily put an end to the nature itself as separate its righteousness from it. We are not made partakers of these righteousnesses; neither of them is put on us to make us just, so that we might live by it. Besides these, there is a righteousness this Person has in the joining of the two natures in one: not the righteousness of his Godhead as distinct from his manhood, nor of his manhood as distinct from his Godhead, but a righteousness that stands in the union of both, and may properly be called the righteousness essential to his being fitted by God for the office of Mediator, the go-between, which he was entrusted with. If he parted with the first righteousness, he would part with his Godhead; if with the second, with the purity of his manhood; if with the third, with the perfection that fits him for the work of mediation. But he has another righteousness besides, which consists in performing, in obeying, the will of God that was revealed to him; and this is the one he puts upon sinners, and by which their sins are covered. That is why it says, ‘As by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.’” [Rom. 5:19]
“But are the other righteousnesses of no use to us?”

“Yes, they are. For though they belong to his natures and his office, and so cannot be passed on to anyone else, it is by their power that the righteousness which makes us right with God is able to do it. The righteousness of his Godhead gives worth to his obedience; the righteousness of his manhood gives his obedience the capacity to justify; and the righteousness that stands in the union of the two natures with his office gives that obedience the authority to do the work it was ordained for.

“So then: here is a righteousness that Christ as God has no need of, for he is God without it; a righteousness that Christ as man has no need of to make him man, for he is perfect man without it; and a righteousness that Christ as God-man has no need of, for he is perfectly that without it. Here, then, is a righteousness that Christ, as God, as man, as God-man, does not need for himself, and so can spare: a justifying righteousness he does not want for himself, and therefore gives away. That is why it is called ‘the gift of righteousness.’ [Rom. 5:17] And since Christ Jesus the Lord placed himself under the law, this righteousness must be given away; for the law binds whoever is under it not only to do justly but to show charity. By the law, a man who has two coats ought to give one to the man who has none. Now our Lord does have two coats, one for himself and one to spare, and so he freely gives one to those who have none. And that, Christiana, and Mercy, and the rest of you here, is how your pardon comes by deed, by the work of another. Your Lord Christ is the One who did the work, and he has given away what he earned to the next poor beggar he met.

“But again, for pardon by deed there must be something paid to God as a price, as well as something prepared to cover us. Sin handed us over to the just curse of a righteous law; from that curse we must be set right by way of redemption, a price paid for the harm we have done [Rom. 4:24]; and that price is the blood of your Lord, who came and stood in your place, and died your death for your transgressions. [Gal. 3:13] So he has ransomed you from your transgressions with his blood, and covered your polluted and deformed souls with righteousness; and for the sake of this, God passes by you, and will not hurt you when he comes to judge the world.”

“This is wonderful,” said Christiana. “Now I see there was something to be learned from our being pardoned by word and by deed. Good Mercy, let us work to keep this in mind; and my children, you remember it too. But sir, wasn’t this what made my good Christian’s burden fall from his shoulders, and made him give three leaps for joy?”
“Yes. It was believing this that cut the cords that could be cut no other way; and it was to give him proof of its power that he was allowed to carry his burden all the way to the Cross.”

“I thought so. For though my heart was light and glad before, it is ten times lighter and gladder now. And I am persuaded by what I have felt, though I have felt only a little as yet, that if the most burdened man in the world were here, and saw and believed as I do now, it would make his heart merry too.”

“It is not only comfort, and the easing of a burden, that comes to us from seeing and considering these things,” said Great-heart, “but a deep love is born in us by them. For who can once think that pardon comes not only by promise, but in this way, and not be moved by the way and means of his redemption, and so by the Man who worked it for him?”

“True. I think it makes my heart bleed to think that he should bleed for me. O loving One! O blessed One! You deserve to have me; you have bought me. You deserve to have all of me; you have paid for me ten thousand times more than I am worth. No wonder this made the tears stand in my husband’s eyes, and made him step out so briskly. I am sure he wished I were with him; but, wretch that I was, I let him come all alone. O Mercy, if only your father and mother were here, and Mrs. Timid too; no, I wish with all my heart that Madam Wanton were here as well. Surely, surely their hearts would be moved; and neither the fear of the one nor the strong lusts of the other could make them turn home again, and refuse to become good pilgrims.”

“You speak now in the warmth of your feelings,” said Great-heart. “Do you think it will always be like this with you? Besides, this is not given to everyone who saw your Jesus bleed. There were those who stood by and saw the blood run from his heart to the ground, and were so far from this that instead of mourning they laughed at him, and instead of becoming his disciples hardened their hearts against him. So all that you have, my daughters, you have by a special impression made by a divine hand, as you reflected on what I have told you. Remember what you were taught, that the hen by her common call gives no food to her chicks. This, then, you have by a special grace.”
